## Logistic Regression

In this section, we try to predict if a person has a coronary heart disease.

### Logistic Regression Without Using Weights

I ignored the various weights in the dataset because I couldn't figure out what they meant and how to use them.
To my surprise, ignoring weights results in models that have ROC = 5.While writing this document, I found out that the previous sentence was wrong. My models were bad because of a bug. In my original code, I intended to train data on the training set that was not defined in the script, and was using another dataframe called __train__ from the global environment. After correcting the bug, the ROC looks normal.


``` {R dataPreparationWithoutWeight, echo = FALSE,include = FALSE}

data = read.csv("cleaned_data.csv")
head(data)

set.seed(123)   # for reproducibility

# First split: train vs rest (2/3 remain)
index1 <- createDataPartition(data$coronary, p = 1/3, list = FALSE)
train <- data[index1, ]
rest  <- data[-index1, ]

# Second split: validation vs test (each 1/3 of full data)
index2 <- createDataPartition(rest$coronary, p = 1/2, list = FALSE)
validation <- rest[index2, ]
test <- rest[-index2, ]

```

I tried to use high_density_level,low_density_level,triglyceride_level as variables. This model didn't work.

``` {R fittingModelWithoutWeightMultiplePredictors, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}

# -----model with multiple predictors-----------.
# 1. Fit on training set
model <- glm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level + low_density_level + triglyceride_level,
  family = binomial,
  data = train
)

# 2. Predict on *validation* set
validation$prob <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = validation,
  type = "response"
)

# 3. ROC on validation set

g <- roc(response = validation$coronary,
         predictor = validation$prob)

g
plot(g)
```

I tried to use only low_density_level.Neither did this model work. 

``` {R fittingModelWithoutWeightOnePredictor, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}
# --------- 1. Fit model on TRAIN only --------------

model <- glm(
  coronary ~ low_density_level,
  family = binomial,
  data = train
)

# --------- 2. Predict on VALIDATION only -----------

validation$prob <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = validation,
  type = "response"
)

# --------- 3. Compute ROC on VALIDATION -----------

library(pROC)

g <- roc(
  response  = validation$coronary,
  predictor = validation$prob
)

g
plot(g)
```


### Logistic Regression With Weights

After the previous trials, I realized the importance of the weights and decided to use them? but how? In order to learn how to use them, I studied NAHNAES's 
sample design, a concept that I haven't studied before and struggled to understand. After having an rudimentary understanding of its sample design, the next challenge is how to choose a weight since there are many weights in the dataset. It took me a while to understand the criteria - choose the weight for the smallest subsample if multiple subsamples are used in the analysis. In my case, I have decide which subsample is smaller because I have two: the phlebotomy subsample(people who gave blood specimen) and the fasting subsample (people who are asked to fast). It took me several hours just to decide on this. Finally, I realized that fasting subsample is smaller because they fasted first and then gave blood specimen. Then, I proceeded to use the fasting weight but the models couldn't converge. After some trials, I used the phlebotomy weight, which finally worked.

```{R loadData,,echo = FALSE,eval = TRUE,include = FALSE}
result = read.csv("cleaned_data_with_weights.csv")
```

#### Logistic Regression With Using Weight_2(Fasting Subsample Weight)

According to NHANES analytic guideline, this weight should be used. However, using fasting weight causes the model fail to converge. The exact reason of the failure requires further study. 

```{R weight2Prepare,,echo = FALSE,eval = TRUE,include = FALSE }
result = subset(result, !is.na(result$weight_2))

design <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~weight_2, # using the smaller subsample weight - fasting weight.
  nest = TRUE,
  data = result
)

```

Trying to fit a model with 3 predictors. This model won't converge.

```{R weight2with3predictors,echo = FALSE,include = FALSE}
# filter out columns with missing values. We shouldn't subset on the df directly.
design_sub <- subset(design,
                     !is.na(coronary) &
                       !is.na(triglyceride_level) &
                       !is.na(high_density_level) &
                       !is.na(low_density_level))
nrow(design_sub)
```

```{R weight2with3predictors2,echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}
model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~  triglyceride_level + high_density_level +low_density_level ,
  design = design_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

```

Trying to fit a model with 1 predictor. This model won't converge either.

```{R weight2with1predictor,echo = FALSE,include = FALSE}

design_sub_2 <- subset(design,
                     !is.na(coronary) &
                       !is.na(triglyceride_level))
```

```{R weight2with1predictor2,echo = TRUE,include = TRUE }

model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~  triglyceride_level,
  design = design_sub_2,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

```

#### Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1(Phlebotomy Subsample Weight)

Since the previous method fails, the Phlebotomy weight is used since it is the weight for the second smallest subsample.

```{R weight1Preparation, echo = FALSE,include = FALSE}

result = subset(result, !is.na(result$weight_1))

# First split: train vs rest (2/3 remain)
index1 <- createDataPartition(result$SEQN, p = 1/3, list = FALSE)
train <- result[index1, ]
rest  <- result[-index1, ]

# Second split: validation vs test (each 1/3 of full data)
index2 <- createDataPartition(rest$SEQN, p = 1/2, list = FALSE)
validation <- rest[index2, ]
test <- rest[-index2, ]

# make the design object for train, validation,test
design_train <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~weight_1, # using the smaller subsample weight - fasting weight.
  nest = TRUE,
  data = train
)


design_validation <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~weight_1, # using the smaller subsample weight - fasting weight.
  nest = TRUE,
  data = validation
)

design_test <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~weight_1, # using the smaller subsample weight - fasting weight.
  nest = TRUE,
  data = test
)

# filter out columns with missing values. 
# We should subset on the design object directly instead of the the dataframe.

design_train_sub <- subset(design_train,
                     !is.na(coronary) &
                       !is.na(high_density_level) &
                       !is.na(low_density_level))
nrow(design_train_sub)

design_validation_sub <- subset(design_validation,
                           !is.na(coronary) &
                             !is.na(high_density_level) &
                             !is.na(low_density_level))
nrow(design_validation_sub)

design_test_sub <- subset(design_test,
                           !is.na(coronary) &
                             !is.na(high_density_level) &
                             !is.na(low_density_level))
nrow(design_test_sub)

```

##### Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1 and Two Predictors

We fit a model using high_density_level and low_density_level. 

```{R regressionWithWeight_1With2Predictors, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}
# --------- model with two predictors -----------------------
# train model on the train set
model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level +low_density_level ,
  design = design_train_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

summary(model)

# predict on the validation set.

val_df <- design_validation_sub$variables
val_df$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = val_df, type = "response")

roc_val_both <- roc(
  response = val_df$coronary,
  predictor = val_df$predicted,
  weights = val_df$weight_1
)

roc_val_both

plot(roc_val_both)

```


##### Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1 and One Predictor

###### With high_density_level

We fit another model with high_density_level.

```{R regressionWithWeight_1With1HDL, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}
# train model on the train set
model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level ,
  design = design_train_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

summary(model)

# predict on the validation set.

val_df <- design_validation_sub$variables
val_df$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = val_df, type = "response")

roc_val_HDL <- roc(
  response = val_df$coronary,
  predictor = val_df$predicted,
  weights = val_df$weight_1
)

roc_val_HDL
plot(roc_val_HDL)

```

###### With low_density_level

We fit another model with low_density_level.

```{R regressionWithWeight_1With1LDL, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}
# train model on the train set
model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~ low_density_level ,
  design = design_train_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

summary(model)

# predict on the validation set.

val_df <- design_validation_sub$variables
val_df$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = val_df, type = "response")

roc_val_LDL <- roc(
  response = val_df$coronary,
  predictor = val_df$predicted,
  weights = val_df$weight_1
)

roc_val_LDL

plot(roc_val_LDL)

```


From this model, we choose a threshhold that yields the highest accuracy.

``` {R name, echo = TRUE,include = TRUE}

# 1.choose the best threshold for this model and calculate the accuracy. 

roc_obj <- roc(response = val_df$coronary, predictor = val_df$predicted)
best <- coords(roc_obj, "best", best.method="closest.topleft")
best

best_threshold <- as.numeric(best$threshold)

# 2. predicted classes using optimal threshold
val_df$predicted_labels <- ifelse(val_df$predicted >= best_threshold[], 1, 0)

# 3. accuracy
accuracy <- mean(val_df$predicted_labels == val_df$coronary)
accuracy
```
